notes:
The self-check's other half: responses production MUST SERVE.

adversarial-responses.json proves the harness can report a FAILURE. It cannot prove the
harness can report a PASS on a response that a guard nearly threw away, and a guard that
refuses a good answer costs the rider exactly as much as one that serves a bad one - more,
because nothing in the pipeline reports it.

Each response here is a real recorded model output that production discarded, or would have.
The run scores every one of them and exits non-zero if any is refused, the mirror of the
adversarial gate above it, and an EMPTY set is the absence of that proof rather than a pass.

THESE GO THROUGH parseAdviceResponse FIRST, and the adversarial fixtures deliberately do not.
That asymmetry is the point of this file: the adversarial set asks what the SCORER does with a
well-formed response, while these ask what the PARSER hands the scorer - which is where a
placeholder stops being a session reference. Scoring these raw would skip the only step under
test. None of the adversarial three carries a value the parser normalizes, so feeding them
through it would change nothing and would quietly alter a gate with its own recorded
provenance.

valid_session_ids is [] for every case, the strictest setting the policy has: with no allowed
ids, ANY non-null source_session_id is unverifiable. A case that passes here passes because the
reference is genuinely absent, not because it happened to match an id in a list.

cases.scenario: Motorcycle gearing: the model answers correctly and writes the string "null" where the session reference belongs.
cases.provenance: tests/fixtures/rag-eval/recordings/completions.json at commit 5524a4c, tape key 5ea2f97b7872510ff6f6d355f4ca5c4d - the golden case mc-gearing-slow-corner, recorded 2026-09-08. The response is verbatim.
cases.what_it_costs_the_rider: evaluateAdvicePolicy reads the four-character string "null" as a session id it cannot verify and force-refuses with invalid_personal_evidence, so a legitimate gearing question returns no advice, no citation and no evidence - only the line that the historical session evidence could not be verified. The answer itself was right: rear_sprocket, decrease, 1 tooth, cited to the gearing file, quoting the rider's own session notes.

response.summary: To address the issue of dropping out of the powerband exiting the second-gear corner, I recommend shortening the gearing by changing the rear sprocket. This should help keep the RPMs within the powerband during your exit.

recommended_changes.reason: Shortening the gearing will help maintain RPMs in the powerband exiting the corner.

safety_notes: This is informational only. You are responsible for vehicle safety and on-track conduct.
Make one change at a time and re-test for a full session before stacking another change.

citations.snippet: Second gear corner that drops RPM below the powerband: shorten gearing.

prediction.expected_effect: Improved acceleration out of the corner and better powerband engagement.
prediction.day_trend: Monitor tire pressures and wear as the day progresses, especially with the current warm conditions.

personal_evidence.label: Session notes
personal_evidence.detail: Falls out of the powerband on the drive out of the slow left. Second gear is too tall there.
